title: He failed 12th grade. He drove a tempo to fund his UPSC prep. He failed that exam three more times. October 9, 2026.
excerpt: From a citizen army created in 1949, to a nonprofit that pays rural women to make their own sanitary pads, October 9's five stories are about capacity built on repeat attempts, not single breakthroughs.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about something that only worked because it was tried more than once - an army model that's held for 77 years, a philanthropic gift that's now its third round at the same university, a nonprofit that retrains its own distributors quarterly, a chip facility built after years of smaller steps, and a man who failed the same exam three times before it worked.

October 9, 1949: India created an army of citizens who kept their day jobs

C. Rajagopalachari formally launched India's Territorial Army under the Territorial Army Act of 1948 - a volunteer 'second line of defence' made up of citizens with regular civilian careers who train for military service. October 9 is still observed as Territorial Army Day, 77 years later.

A couple gave their US university $20 million. It became a college named for them - built entirely around AI

Vikas and Anuradha Sinha gave the University of North Texas $20 million to launch the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics - their third gift to the same university since 2024, after earlier gifts created its Department of Data Science and Innovation Lab.

Her nonprofit trains rural women to make and sell their own sanitary pads

Megha Desai, President of The Desai Foundation, runs the Asani Sanitary Napkin Program across 8 Indian states - training roughly 250 local women as paid distributors rather than handing out free pads, reaching millions of lives and earning recognition at the 2022 Clinton Global Initiative.

India just started testing the memory chips going into your next laptop

Micron's $2.75 billion Sanand, Gujarat facility - India's first commercial semiconductor assembly and test plant - opened February 28, 2026, and immediately shipped its first made-in-India memory modules to Dell, scaling toward hundreds of millions of chips a year by 2027.

He failed his 12th-grade board exam. He drove a tempo to fund his UPSC studies. He failed the exam itself three more times

Manoj Kumar Sharma worked as a tempo driver and library assistant to fund his UPSC preparation after failing his board exams, then failed the civil services exam three times before clearing it on his fourth attempt with All India Rank 121 - his story later becoming the film '12th Fail.'

Five stories, one thread: an army model still running after 77 years, a gift that kept compounding at the same institution, a nonprofit that keeps retraining its own workers, a chip facility that scaled up in stages, and a man whose fourth attempt was the one that worked. Nothing here succeeded on the first try - all of it succeeded anyway.
